Note for testing, you can use https://github.com/godotengine/godot-demo-projects/tree/master/xr/mobile_vr_interface_demo to test stereoscopic functionality.

I'm also working on this little demo project that lets you play with various projections and see whats going on:

[test-projections.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25377977/test-projections.zip)
cc @huwpascoe, finally getting around to doing my version of this. I'm far from finished and have still to go through issues I flagged on your original PR. we'll see where we get to ;)

> solved our shadow shaking issue

Tested with the MobileVRInterface and it does seem to fix #84510 for XR, the jitter is gone. This is consistent with our findings, but remember that I can still reproduce the issue with a Camera3D under certain conditions.

I've also tried setting the projection matrix of a Camera3D and that works nicely so far. Will get back to you with further testing of that feature, especially for XR portals and mirrors that I am a big fan of.

> Tested with the MobileVRInterface and it does seem to fix #84510 for XR, the jitter is gone. This is consistent with our findings, but remember that I can still reproduce the issue with a Camera3D under certain conditions.

Owh I definitely think there is more going on but this PR does fix the stability issue with how the combined frustum is calculated, which is being used to determine the center point of the shadow cascades. 

In the old solution it's actually some distance behind the head where the two eye frustums meet.

I took some time to improve the test project I made, which can now be found here: https://codeberg.org/BastiaanOlij/test-projections I purposefully added a few things that I knew are broken as we only work around them when stereo rendering is enabled: The main one that is immediately obvious is SDFGI, where things are offset. But there are others that are equally problematic. Less visible as I'm testing fog, the sky is wrong as it is still centered. These are all variations around unprojecting screen coordinates through an optimisation which does not work for asymmetrical projection matrices. So the next step is to find all the effected places and instead of checking for stereo, checking for asymmetrical projections. This will likely solve many other use cases that have previously prevented us from offering more freedom around projection matrices.

Spend a bunch of time investigating a number of issues that challenged a few preconceptions I've held for a while. There are a number of issues introduced with stereo rendering that I thought were related to asymmetrical projection matrices but are in fact caused by the way we handle our stereo offset. However with giving users the freedom to submit any projection matrix, we're still going to need to deal with these situations better. Now before we look into that further, I lost a lot of time on SDFGI only to come to the conclusion that it's likely been broken for asymmetrical projection matrices for some time, unrelated to the changes I'm making here. Note here with our built-in frustum camera and zero offset, the back wall of our little hut is dark: But move the offset by 1cm and we see that things no longer line up: If you line up the before and after images, you'll see that screenspace wise the SDFGI data is still centered on screen. There is another issue I ran into when the floor is metallic, first it highlights the shift even better, but also, that looks very broken (and again, not related to this PR) :) I'll get to SDFGI later and if I can't figure it out, I'll make sure to raise some bugs.

So back on the topic of asymmetrical, so I'm now testing the new logic by setting up a single projection matrix. A projection matrix is asymmetrical when the field of view on the left is different from the right, or the top different from the bottom, which is very normal in XR scenarios, but also happens when you're dealing with things like projection matrices for screen space slanted mirrors. Note here the "skew" applied to x and y as a factor of z (I've enabled SSAO here and cranked it up a bit): Note that even though the camera is dead center in front of the Godot cube, our cube is to the right of the image. Just for contrast, if we render our right eye we get the opposite effect: I was expecting things to look broken but they actually look correct. I always made the assumption this was due to the asymmetrical projection as in various places, we take a shortcut in unprojecting. In order to unproject a screen space coordinate, where we're only interested in the original X and Y coordinates, we only need four values from our projection matrix for basically any projection matrix: And that is what our "shortcut" code uses. However, we're missing an ingredient here. In stereo rendering our eye is offset from our camera position by half our IPD. As an optimisation we encode this offset into our projection matrix. Now we get the following situation: These values that do effect the X and Y coordinate, aren't taken into account into the unprojection. We don't see any issues however. Our sky is projected to infinity, so a 3cm shift of the camera is not going to matter (as I previously made the mistake that the 3rd row wasn't taken into account, which does alter the results greatly, I often thought it would). The red line is right where it should be. I've still applied the fix just to be safe here. However anything being unprojected that is in the foreground will be misplaced. I was hoping SSAO would be one of those effects but I think that is just rendered in screen space, it doesn't actually do an unproject. The fix here btw is that we are checking if any of these values are none-zero and triggering a full unproject if that is the case: I just wanted to document the reasoning and what we need to chase in order to fix effects that are misbehaving. Now the hunt starts for finding the actual situations where this is going wrong.

The more I think about this, the more this is a problem. The unprojection in our current stereoscopic implementation works because we add our camera offset later and keep that transform.

When doing a full unproject, your vertex position is in relation to the center position of the players head, and to get the actual unprojected value we need, we add the offset back in.

If we just have a projection matrix with the eye offset (which can also include a rotation), but we don't have the offset transform, we're missing a vital ingredient.

Now the new API allows us to both provide the projection matrix and the offset, and applies the offset inside of the rendering engine,

I'm wondering if we should make a limitation that we only accept projection matrices where `[0][1]`, `[1][0]`, `[3][0]` and `[3][1]` are all zero and force the user to use the offset transform.

This would greatly reduce the risk of projection matrices being introduced that break.

@BastiaanOlij Sorry if this information is redundant, but isn't that the same problem that [godotengine/godot-proposals#11436](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11436) addressed? He claimed that for any practical use of a custom projection matrix, the user would not have to set those to anything but zero, so the matrix should not be exposed bare, but have setters that still allow for all manipulation necessary for any real use case. I believe he also explained why these should always be zero.

As a side note, I'm excited on the progress of this PR because it's currently impossible to achieve an accurate oblique clip distance for portals, and custom matrix would fix that.

The SDFGI issues turn out to be unrelated to this work and a problem that has existed for awhile yet. Raised a separate issue because I just can't figure out where it's going wrong. All I know is that back in Godot 4.0/4.1 days I had it working at some point (or maybe I never realised the issues):

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/117303

Ok, so I added in the ability to select the tracking on `XRCamera3D`, that has been a long outstanding task. I do want to extend this with an API on `XRInterface` so interfaces can specify which trackers they support.

I'm contemplating introducing a `XRHeadTracker` subclass of `XRPositionalTracker` that adds access to the projection matrix data and remove the `first_view` and `last_view` properties I added. That would be a much cleaner solution.
Discussing this with the XR team.
Finally figured out the issues with SDFGI, fixed in #117619 which will be included in this PR as well.

Had discussion during the XR meeting about whether to move input function from 'XRPositionalTracker' to 'XRControllerTracker' now that we want to introduce 'XRCameraTracker'. @lyuma noted that there are headsets with inputs and haptics on the headset itself and that in theory interaction profiles could become available in the future that would allow us to have inputs and outputs on `XRCameraTracker`. May be prudent to keep the status quo but add a remark in the `XRPositionalTracker` documentation.

The idea around `XRCameraTracker` ran into a snag, after discussing with the team today we're going to change the approach slightly. We'll keep using the tracker names idea but will add an API to `XRServer`/`XRInterface` to obtain projection and offset data.

The main blocker was around near/far settings on each camera which is data unknown inside of the `XRInterface` in our current approach.

Added in the foundation of the changed API as discussed with @dsnopek and @m4gr3d 

`XRInterface.get_view_offset` will be removed, just keeping it for now as I still need to use the code fragments. Still need to implement the new logic on the actual interfaces and on `XRInterfaceExtension`.

`XRCamera3D` now calls `get_camera_projections` and `get_camera_offsets` on our `XRServer`. The `XRServer` will find the first active `XRInterface` that can return this information (prioritising our primary interface).

By default most `XRInterface`s will support the tracker called `head` which will track the headset the user wears.
Systems that support multiple users may introduce additional trackers for each player (see TiltFive, which will need to be adjusted).
Other examples are:
- adding support for a 3rd person camera as part of OpenXRs [XR_MSFT_first_person_observer](https://registry.khronos.org/OpenXR/specs/1.1/html/xrspec.html#XR_MSFT_first_person_observer) extension
- adding support for OpenXRs `XR_VIEW_CONFIGURATION_TYPE_PRIMARY_STEREO_WITH_FOVEATED_INSET` where the camera is in the same position but with different projection matrices and potentially different offsets.

I just wanted to pitch in and say that this PR has been absolutely rock solid. I've been using it as my daily for quite some time with no issues to report. I've attached a quick little video showcasing some custom rendering using projections. I hope to see this PR merged!

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9816241a-74f2-4f22-b39d-649492293ea1

It is vital to my game project, where it swaps between a top-down 2D perspective and a 3D perspective. I'm not operating on this PR specifically because I don't want to go through recompiling the engine and updating my code until an official release comes out, but this feature and PR have my support.

> This needs to be scoped better to be an XR-specific feature. Right now it is an XR refactor pretending to be a general-purpose rendering feature. In reality, this is a code cleanup that makes the XR codepath a bit more flexible
> 
> It looks like a helpful drop-in for building the XR projection matrices and allows you to slightly simplify the XR codepath in the renderer, but the API looks almost the same as the custom matrix proposal that people are very excited about, but it doesn't implement custom matrices at all.
> 
> To be mergable, this needs to be scoped better. At minimum, the API needs to change from `camera_set_projections()` to `camera_set_xr_projections()`. The associated naming (enums, properties, etc.) should be updated as well.

@clayjohn not sure why you conclude this, while my use case is driven by XR needs, this PR has much wider usage. To be exact, I think there is a follow up path to simplify the way `Camera3D` works and steer everything through `camera_set_projection` and retire the other `camera_set_*` functions.

I just wanted to draw a line to not make this more complex than it needs to be (see also my remarks on this in my original description), and that the camera options we expose to normal users will always stay curated to communicate only power users who directly interact with the rendering server can set their own projection matrices.

I've taken specific care to test if various custom matrices work and that effects in Godot support them (hence finding and fixing bugs in several effects). I can't guarantee I've found all issues but I'm confident they can be fixed quickly.
I've also added checks in to give an error if a projection matrix is supplied that breaks rendering.

But bottom line is, this is not an XR centric feature and I think we're shooting ourselves in the foot if we do this rename.

To be exact, I think there is a follow up path to simplify the way `Camera3D` works and steer everything through `camera_set_projection` and retire the other `camera_set_*` functions.

This code doesn't touch any codepaths other than replacing the existing XR codepath. Plus the API only makes sense for XR cameras. It pretends to be a general purpose API, but if you use it for anything except for XR, it will completely break. 

Plus it clashes with our plans to have a custom camera matrix support. This is a worse API for non-XR cases than the one we agreed upon, but it is named such that there won't be room to actually implement custom project matrices without naming it something really awkward and making the API super messy.

I can't guarantee I've found all issues but I'm confident they can be fixed quickly. I've also added checks in to give an error if a projection matrix is supplied that breaks rendering.

Again, it looks like the only code path that you have actually touched is the custom XR projection matrix code path.

I tested most of those and they actually work. I've explained in detail up above why we thought there were problems that weren't actually there. Where fixes were needed these were in separate PRs that have already been merged.

The only one I will give you is ray casting in the sense that we're not changing Camera3D, and Camera3D will thus not be aware of a changed projection matrix with which to give you a proper ray origin and ray direction. That is something I think is defendable when people bypass things and set things directly on the rendering server (as is the case with many such options), though sometime in the future I'd like to make some changes on the node side of things.

Now it's definitely possible I've missed testing things or improperly tested things. I will admit that I need to take another look at the temporal reprojection implementations but seeing they all work on the projection matrix, they should work within the constraints enforced here
.
There are some effects that simply don't work in a stereo situation, but that is already the case regardless of this change and is unrelated to the projection matrix used, but due to stereoscopic changing how these effects need to be implemented.

I'd love for more feedback from people and people actually testing this and pointing out the issues. But as you can see there have been plenty of people testing this and not finding them.

That said, we should probably mark the function as experimental, because there are bound to be things found once this is out in the wild, and there are bound to be things people do that will never work nor should work. But that is why this is not exposed in the node system.

> I tested most of those and they actually work. I've explained in detail up above why we thought there were problems that weren't actually there. Where fixes were needed these were in separate PRs that have already been merged.

Almost of those effects will break if you use a non-perspective projection. Many of them also have a fast path for purely orthogonal/purely projective and will break with anything blended. 

The problem with doing this without proper support is that it will appear to work okay for very simple test cases but will be totally broken when users go to actually use it for their game. 

If you look at the original PR adding the custom matrix you can see how much code Juan added for a W4 customer who needed it for their game. And even then, Juan only added company code for the effects the customer needed. 

That original PR did what this PR does, it just allowed users to override the projection matrix without handling any of the effects. And it completely failed for games that actually needed it. So I have no doubt this will be the same. Those problems won't magically go away. We either handle the case of custom projection matrices, or we do nothing. But we absolutely cannot merge something that only appears to work as long as real projects don't attempt to use it

Ah yes, that applies to my situation as well but I specifically state that in my introduction. As we're overriding the projection matrix on the rendering server, the Camera3D node and all the functionality related to it is none the wiser, and that is a given restriction of where we stand today.

The long term I'd like to clean up how we structure Camera3D to something like this:
```
- BaseCamera3D
  - Camera3D
  - XRCamera3D
  - CustomCamera3D
```

Where:
- `BaseCamera3D` simply becomes a template class that defines the API of the rest of the engine into our camera system.
- `Camera3D` is our user facing camera as it is today, with no more functionality than it has today, with just the existing camera modes, but likely using the `set_camera_projection` method to set the projection matrix on the rendering side so we clean up a lot of duplicate code.
- `XRCamera3D` is our XR camera that sets stereo projections, and as it stands today, does not have a working ray casting implementation because our current solution isn't compatible with stereo rendering.
- `CustomCamere3D` isn't a node in Godot, instead just an example of how someone wanting a custom projection matrix needs to implement their own camera implementation, either in GDScript or as a GDExtension. The developer will be responsible for not just setting the projection matrix, but also implementing any related logic around this. Obviously by exposing the right functions on our Projection matrix class we can make this easier, but in the end making raycasting work will be part of the responsibility of whomever implements a custom camera.

It was never my intension that we allow a developer to set an arbitrary projection matrix on `Camera3D` and magically expect stuff like raycasting to work. 

I just wanted to do the node side restructure separate from the rendering changes because this stuff becomes complex enough already.

**edit**, this btw is why it would be good if we can have our US time rendering meetings again, I feel like we would nail this in a quick call. I'm sure I'm over looking scenarios, but at the same time I think there are a lot of scenarios I have already looked into.

Just a quick update on this. visionPro changes were made but still hunting some bugs. Hopefully will be able to complete it early this week.

Ok, some more info, figured out what was going wrong with the visionOS XR changes. Turned out the code was actually sound but the projection matrices the AVP returns have a slight rotation embedded in them that doesn't pass my added checks.

Seeing this would only potentially impact some high end effects on Forward+, and we've now renamed the new rendering APIs to be specific for XR, I'm wondering if we should remove the check.

That said, I'm looking into this further to see if we can tune the check or if something can  be done on the AVP side.

For anyone that wants to have a look, or test, I've parked the changes here:
https://github.com/BastiaanOlij/godot/tree/projection_camera_vpro
I will be updating this PR after I have some more feedback.

I want to test some more but I've removed the checks on the projections as they were too strict for HMDs that have skewed panels.

This does open the door wider for developers to submit projection matrices that will not work well, and there will be some features in Forward+ that may cause issues on hardware like Vision Pro.

With that requirement, @clayjohn call to rename the methods specific for `xr` definately was the right call. Also suggest we keep the new method marked as experimental until we have a clearer picture of what rendering effects may need further tweaks and whether we can come up with a more fitting test for unsupported scenarios.
